intro: One-page lesson outlines for classrooms and debate prep. Each brief links into pages we already publish — no invented collation data. Greek NT word-level compare stays on /compare/ (CNTR only); other traditions use timeline cards and curated tables.

briefs.title: What is a variation unit?
briefs.subtitle: Word-aligned disagreements vs a base text
briefs.audience: Students · debaters · first visit to Coverage
briefs.learning_goal: Define a variation unit the way this site counts it (extant Greek letters aligned to SR GNT), and separate that from block-level famous passages or tradition-scale estimates.

steps.text: Read the Coverage primer on what Ehrman asked, what Gurry estimated, and what our mechanical census actually covers.
Open the variant explorer and filter by kind (omission, substitution, orthography, etc.) — each row is one counted unit in extant text.
On a witness card, read the strip under a verse: that is the same unit logic at single-verse scale.
Contrast with Famous passages: whole verses or pericopes missing or added — taught as block issues, not mixed into the word census.

briefs.dont_overclaim: Our ~37k-style totals count word-aligned units in a bounded 1–400 CE CNTR slice vs SR GNT — not Gurry’s ~500,000 across the full Greek tradition, and not Qurʾān or LXX material.

briefs.title: Famous block omissions and additions
briefs.subtitle: Pericope Adulterae, Mark’s ending, Comma Johanneum, and more
briefs.learning_goal: Use block-level famous passages to argue precisely about what early Greek witnesses contain or omit — without treating them as rows in the word-level variant census.

steps.text: Skim the ten curated famous passage cards and note which witnesses CNTR marks absent vs present.
Cross-check a claim card (e.g. Pericope Adulterae in P66, P75, 01, 03) against the famous entry and the underlying witness cards.

links.label: Claim: PA absent in early witnesses

steps.text: When someone cites “thousands of variants,” redirect: block omissions are real but counted differently from spelling disagreements in Coverage.

briefs.dont_overclaim: Famous cards document status in our CNTR slice and curated scholarship links — not every manuscript ever copied, and not automatic proof about authorial originals.

briefs.title: Uthmanic regional rasm ≠ “40 different Qurans”
briefs.subtitle: Graphic stemma vs content rewrites
briefs.learning_goal: Explain regional rasm differences within the Uthmanic Text Type using our illustrative table — and reject both “zero variation” and “forty conflicting Qurans” slogans.

steps.text: Read the Uthmanic regional rasm page: ~35–40 published graphic differences among exemplar traditions, with sources — not a full mushaf census.
Open the claim cards on zero variation vs seventh-century stability.
Contrast UT rasm with the Ṣanʿāʾ palimpsest lower text — one card, two layers, not a verse-alignment compare tool.
Browse Hijazi catalog witnesses on the Qurʾān timeline for dated leaves and library metadata (no invented collation).

briefs.dont_overclaim: Our 40 rasm rows cite published stemmatics; they do not prove or disprove theological claims about preservation, and they are not parallel-verse alignments like Greek NT compare.

briefs.title: Rasm ≠ qirāʾāt ≠ Ṣanʿāʾ lower text
briefs.subtitle: Stop conflating orthography, reading traditions, and the palimpsest
briefs.audience: Islamic studies · interfaith debate · anyone citing our Qurʾān charts
briefs.learning_goal: Name three separate categories — Uthmanic rasm (what our tables show), canonical qirāʾāt (reading-tradition scholarship we do not census), and Ṣanʿāʾ DAM 01-27.1 lower text (non-UT companion line) — and use claim cards when debaters merge them.

steps.text: Read the plain-English guide and skim the three-column “supports / does not support” matrix.
Open claim cards for the two most common conflations: regional rasm vs Seven/Ten qirāʾāt, and Ṣanʿāʾ lower text vs “UT is fiction.”
Optional third card: undotted early script does not make every reading equally original.
Pair with our published rasm layers — regional splits and shared niʿmat orthography — not a qirāʾāt table.
Open the Ṣanʿāʾ witness card: upper UT-type layer vs lower companion text (Sadeghi & Goudarzi 2012).

briefs.dont_overclaim: We do not host qirāʾāt variant lists or a full mushaf collation — cite Nasser, Shah handbook chapters, and van Putten for reading traditions; cite our JSON only for rasm teaching rows.

briefs.title: Three Qurʾān evidence layers on this site
briefs.subtitle: Timeline cards · regional rasm · shared idiosyncrasies
briefs.audience: Islamic studies · interfaith debate · new contributors
briefs.learning_goal: Route users to the correct page for each kind of Qurʾān evidence — and avoid conflating regional splits, written-archetype arguments, and non-Uthmanic palimpsest layers.

steps.text: Layer 1: open the Qurʾān timeline for dated Hijazi witness cards (metadata and licensed images — not a full mushaf collation).
Layer 2: regional Uthmanic rasm — ~40 places Cook/Sidky report the four exemplar traditions differ.
Layer 3: shared orthographic idiosyncrasies — niʿmat ta vs ta marbūṭa matrix (van Putten 2019 Table 2) for the written-archetype argument.
Keep Ṣanʿāʾ’s lower text separate: one card, two layers, not UT — and keep qirāʾāt separate from rasm.
Check claim cards before citing the matrix in debate.

briefs.dont_overclaim: The niʿmat table reproduces one published case study — not a generated variant census of the whole Qurʾān, and not proof about who personally standardized the rasm.

briefs.title: Three Hebrew Bible evidence traditions on this site
briefs.subtitle: DSS Hebrew · Masoretic Text · Septuagint
briefs.audience: Hebrew Bible survey · LXX/MT debates · NT background
briefs.learning_goal: Route students to the Hebrew/LXX evidence map and timeline cards — distinguishing Qumran Hebrew, late MT standardization, and early Jewish Greek without collapsing them into one “original Bible” line.

steps.text: Open the evidence map page: three cards with short essays and witness deep links.
Tradition 1 — switch to the Hebrew/LXX timeline and open 1QIsaᵃ (Great Isaiah Scroll).
Tradition 2 — read the MT essay: medieval standard, not what Jesus held as a printed codex.
Tradition 3 — open pre-Christian LXX papyri (P.Ryl. 458, P.Fouad 266) and related claim cards.
Keep Greek NT compare separate: CNTR 1–400 CE only — no built-in LXX↔NT collation.

briefs.dont_overclaim: Our 24 Hebrew/LXX cards are illustrative seeds with diplomatic excerpts — not BHQ or Göttingen apparatus dumps, not a DSS↔MT verse census, and not proof that MT or LXX alone equals “what Jesus read” for every book.

briefs.title: Dead Sea Scrolls Hebrew vs medieval Masoretic Text
briefs.subtitle: Earlier diversity, later standardization
briefs.learning_goal: Use 1QIsaᵃ and related cards to show pre-Masoretic Hebrew diversity without claiming the DSS replace BHQ or that LXX equals “the original.”

steps.text: Switch the timeline to Hebrew Bible & LXX (250 BCE–400 CE) and open the Great Isaiah Scroll card.
Read the diplomatic excerpt notes on the card — compare wording to the display English (WEB), not a full apparatus.
Add Nash Papyrus or Murabbaʿat examples for pre-Masoretic spellings vs later MT codices.
Keep Greek NT compare separate: LXX papyri on this site are their own cards, not CNTR verse alignment.

briefs.dont_overclaim: We host illustrative excerpts and images where licensed — not Leon Levy/IAA full plates, not BHQ or Göttingen apparatus dumps, and no automated DSS↔MT verse census.

briefs.title: Nag Hammadi vs the Greek NT canon stream
briefs.subtitle: Fourth-century Coptic codices, not lost Matthew manuscripts
briefs.learning_goal: Describe what Nag Hammadi codices are physically and literarily — and refute equating them with the Greek NT manuscript tradition this site collates.

steps.text: Open the Nag Hammadi corpus on the timeline (18 tractate witnesses in our seed).
Read the Gospel of Thomas card and note Coptic Scriptorium diplomatic text — overlap with Greek sayings tradition is scholarly, not a built-in Thomas↔John compare.
Pair mentally with an early Greek gospel fragment on the NT timeline (e.g. P52) — two routes, not one collation engine.
Use the claim card before arguing “lost books of the Bible.”

briefs.dont_overclaim: Nag Hammadi images and excerpts illustrate non-canonical Coptic Christianity; they do not enumerate how many “versions” of Matthew existed in Greek.

briefs.title: How to cite this site
briefs.subtitle: Website, census downloads, and curated JSON
briefs.learning_goal: Cite Illustrative Manuscripts for what we actually publish (bounded Greek census, curated tables, catalog metadata) and point readers to CNTR/INTF for primaries.

steps.text: Copy Chicago/MLA/BibTeX templates for the site and open downloads.
If you quote disagreement totals, cite variant-census.json/csv and state the 1–400 CE CNTR scope.
For famous passages or Uthmani rasm, cite the dedicated JSON files with entry counts from the cite page.
Route classmates through teaching briefs instead of misquoting charts.

briefs.dont_overclaim: Do not cite our Greek disagreement total as “the number of NT variants in history,” or our 40 rasm examples as a complete Qurʾān variant catalog.
